tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Interpret each convolution output value as the signed area of the product over the $\tau$-interval where $x(\tau)$ overlaps the flipped-shifted impulse response $h(t-\tau)$.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Convolution as Overlap Area

image_slots.image_description: A clean instructional convolution-overlap diagram on a shared $\tau$-axis. Show a simple positive rectangular $x(\tau)$ pulse and a simple positive rectangular flipped-shifted $h(t0-\tau)$ pulse for one fixed output time $t=t0$. Shade only the interval where the two rectangles overlap. Below them, show the product $x(\tau)$$h(t0-\tau)$ as one positive rectangle over the same overlap interval. Label the shaded product area as $y(t0)$. Include clear labels for $\tau$, $x(\tau)$, $h(t0-\tau)$, $x(\tau)$$h(t0-\tau)$, the overlap interval, and the area that becomes $y(t0)$. Keep the signals simple and avoid moving-t case boundaries or a full convolution-output plot.

blocks.text: The convolution integral can be read as an area calculation when the output time is fixed. For one chosen value of t, $\tau$ is the variable that runs along the signal timeline.

At that fixed output time, the two factors $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$ only contribute on $\tau$-values where both signals are nonzero. Outside their overlap, at least one factor is zero, so the product contributes no area.

On the overlap interval, multiply the two signal values point by point. This creates the product signal $x(\tau)$$h(t-\tau)$. The signed area under that product, measured along the $\tau$-axis, is the single output value for the chosen time.

If the product is above the axis, its area adds to $y(t)$. If the product is below the axis, its area subtracts from $y(t)$. If there is no overlap, the product is zero everywhere, so that output value is zero.
In this lesson, the main task is to read convolution output values from overlap area. The focus is the area of the product for one fixed output time, not the full piecewise convolution curve.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Product Area for a Fixed Output Time

image_slots.image_description: Two aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared $\tau$-axis for fixed output time $t=2$. Top plot: $x(\tau)=1 on 0\le\tau\le3 and 0 elsewhere$. Middle plot: $h(2-\tau)=2 on 1\le\tau\le4 and 0 elsewhere$. Shade the overlap interval $1\le\tau\le3 on both plots$. Bottom product-area panel: show $x(\tau)$$h(2-\tau)=2 on 1\le\tau\le3 and 0 elsewhere as a rectangle of width 2 and height 2$, shaded and labeled area = $4 = y(2)$. Include $\tau$-axis labels and endpoints 0, 1, 3, and 4.

example_content.example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=2$, a graph shows $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau\le 3$ and $h(2-\tau)=2$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Interpret $y(2)$ as an overlap area.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that $t$ is already fixed at 2. That means $h(2-\tau)$ is a fixed shifted response, and the only variable being scanned is $\tau$.
Read the two nonzero intervals from the graph. The input $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0\le \tau\le 3$, and the shifted response $h(2-\tau)$ is nonzero on $1\le \tau\le 4$.
The product can be nonzero only where both intervals are active. The common part is $1\le \tau\le 3$.
On that overlap, $x(\tau)=1$ and $h(2-\tau)=2$, so the product height is 2. The overlap width is $3-1=2$.
The output value $y(2)$ is the signed area under the product over the overlap interval. Here the product is positive, so the area is positive.
So for this fixed output time, the overlap area gives $y(2)=4$.

sections.section_title: Reading Positive Overlap Area from Two Positive Signals

image_slots.image_description: Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared $\tau$-axis for fixed output time $t=3$. Top plot: $x(\tau)=2 on 0\le\tau\le4 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely above the axis. Middle plot: $h(3-\tau)=1 on 1\le\tau\le3 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely above the axis. Shade the overlap interval $1\le\tau\le3 on both plots$. Bottom product-area panel: show $x(\tau)$$h(3-\tau)=2 on 1\le\tau\le3 and 0 elsewhere as a rectangle above the axis with width 2$, height 2, and positive area label $+4 = y(3)$. Include $\tau$-axis labels and endpoints 0, 1, 3, and 4.

example_content.example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=3$, a graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 4$ and $h(3-\tau)=1$ on $1\le \tau\le 3$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Use the overlap area to find $y(3)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that both plotted signals are above the axis wherever they overlap. When both signal values are positive, their product is positive, so the overlap area adds to the convolution output.
Read the overlap interval from the two supports. The signal $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0\le \tau\le 4$, and $h(3-\tau)$ is nonzero on $1\le \tau\le 3$. Their common interval is $1\le \tau\le 3$.
On this overlap, the heights are $x(\tau)=2$ and $h(3-\tau)=1$. Multiplying two positive heights gives a positive product height.
The product rectangle has width $3-1=2$ and height 2. Because the rectangle is above the axis, its signed area is positive.
So the positive overlap area contributes $+4$, and the convolution output at this fixed time is $y(3)=4$.

sections.section_title: Accounting for Signed Area When the Product Is Negative

image_slots.image_description: Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared $\tau$-axis for fixed output time $t=1$. Top plot: $x(\tau)=2 on 0\le\tau\le3 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely above the axis. Middle plot: $h(1-\tau)=-1 on 1\le\tau\le4 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely below the axis on its support. Shade the overlap interval $1\le\tau\le3 on both plots$. Bottom product-area panel: show $x(\tau)$$h(1-\tau)=-2 on 1\le\tau\le3 and 0 elsewhere as a rectangle below the axis with width 2$, height -2, and signed area label $-4 = y(1)$. Include $\tau$-axis labels and endpoints 0, 1, 3, and 4.

example_content.example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=1$, a graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 3$ and $h(1-\tau)=-1$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Use the signed overlap area to find $y(1)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the two overlapping signal values have opposite signs. The overlap area is still found the same way as before, but the product lies below the axis, so its signed area is negative.
Read the two nonzero intervals from the graph. The input $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0\le \tau\le 3$, and the shifted response $h(1-\tau)$ is nonzero on $1\le \tau\le 4$.
On the overlap, $x(\tau)=2$ is positive and $h(1-\tau)=-1$ is negative. The sign of the area comes from the sign of their product.
The product rectangle has width $3-1=2$ and height $-2$. Since the product is below the axis, the signed area is negative.
So the signed overlap area contributes $-4$, and the convolution output at this fixed time is $y(1)=-4$.

sections.section_title: Comparing Output Values from Different Amounts of Overlap

image_slots.image_description: Two side-by-side fixed-output-time panels on shared $\tau$-axes. In both panels, show the same $x(\tau)=1 on 1\le\tau\le4 and 0 elsewhere$. Left panel labeled $t=1$: show $h(1-\tau)=2 on -1\le\tau\le2 and 0 elsewhere$, shade overlap $1\le\tau\le2$, and show a product-area rectangle $x(\tau)$$h(1-\tau)=2 on 1\le\tau\le2 with area 2 labeled y(1)=2$. Right panel labeled $t=3$: show $h(3-\tau)=2 on 1\le\tau\le4 and 0 elsewhere$, shade overlap $1\le\tau\le4$, and show a product-area rectangle $x(\tau)$$h(3-\tau)=2 on 1\le\tau\le4 with area 6 labeled y(3)=6$. Use matching positive colors for product regions above the axis and include a comparison label $y(3)>y(1)$.

example_content.example_prompt: Two panels show the same input $x(\tau)=1$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$ with $h(1-\tau)=2$ on $-1\le \tau\le 2$ in the first panel and $h(3-\tau)=2$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$ in the second panel, with all signals zero elsewhere. Compare $y(1)$ and $y(3)$ by comparing the two overlap areas.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that each panel represents a different fixed output time. Use the same signed-area rule in each panel, then compare the resulting product areas.
For the first panel, the fixed output time is $t=1$. The input is active on $1\le \tau\le 4$, while $h(1-\tau)$ is active on $-1\le \tau\le 2$, so the overlap is $1\le \tau\le 2$.
On that overlap, the product height is $1\cdot 2=2$. The overlap width is $2-1=1$, so the signed product area is positive and equals 2.
For the second panel, the fixed output time is $t=3$. The same input is active on $1\le \tau\le 4$, and $h(3-\tau)$ is also active on $1\le \tau\le 4$, so the overlap is wider.
The product height is still $1\cdot 2=2$, but the overlap width is $4-1=3$. That gives a larger positive product area.
Both product areas are positive, so the larger area gives the larger output value. Therefore, $y(3)>y(1)$.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero Output from No Overlap Area

image_slots.image_description: Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared $\tau$-axis for fixed output time $t=5$. Top plot: $x(\tau)$ is supported on $0\le\tau\le2 and zero elsewhere$. Middle plot: $h(5-\tau)$ is supported on $3\le\tau\le4 and zero elsewhere$. Leave a visible gap between $\tau=2 and \tau=3 and label it no overlap$. Do not shade any common interval. Bottom product-area panel: show $x(\tau)$$h(5-\tau)=0 for all \tau$, with no product rectangle and a label area = $0 = y(5)$. Include $\tau$-axis labels and endpoints 0, 2, 3, and 4.

example_content.example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=5$, a graph shows $x(\tau)$ supported on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(5-\tau)$ supported on $3\le \tau\le 4$. Use overlap area to determine $y(5)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the two nonzero support intervals are separated. The output does not come from the area of either individual signal; it comes from the signed area of the product where both signals are nonzero at the same $\tau$-values.
Read the two supports from the graph. The input $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $0\le \tau\le 2$, and the shifted response $h(5-\tau)$ is nonzero only on $3\le \tau\le 4$.

explanation_blocks.latex: x(\tau)\ne 0\text{ only on }0\le \tau\le 2,\qquad h(5-\tau)\ne 0\text{ only on }3\le \tau\le 4

explanation_blocks.text: These intervals do not overlap. There is a gap between the end of the support of $x(\tau)$ and the start of the support of $h(5-\tau)$.
Since there is no $\tau$-value where both factors are nonzero, their product is zero for every value of $\tau$.
The signed area under a product that is zero everywhere is zero. Therefore the convolution output at this fixed time is $y(5)=0$.

Middle plot: $h(1-\tau)=1 on -1\le\tau\le1 and 0 elsewhere$. Shade the overlap interval $0\le\tau\le1 on both plots$. Bottom product-area panel: show $x(\tau)$$h(1-\tau)=2 on 0\le\tau\le1 and 0 elsewhere as a shaded rectangle of width 1 and height 2$. Include $\tau$-axis labels and endpoints -1, 0, 1, and 2. Two aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared $\tau$-axis for fixed output time $t=4$. Top plot: $x(\tau)=3 on 1\le\tau\le4 and 0 elsewhere$. Middle plot: $h(4-\tau)=2 on 2\le\tau\le5 and 0 elsewhere$. Shade the overlap interval $2\le\tau\le4 on both plots$. Bottom product-area panel: show $x(\tau)$$h(4-\tau)=6 on 2\le\tau\le4 and 0 elsewhere as a shaded rectangle of width 2 and height 6$. Include $\tau$-axis labels and endpoints 1, 2, 4, and 5. prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=1$, the graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(1-\tau)=1$ on $-1\le \tau\le 1$, with both signals zero elsewhere.
Use the overlap area to find $y(1)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The common nonzero interval is $0\le \tau\le 1$, so the overlap width is 1. On that interval, the product height is $2\cdot 1=2$, giving area $2\cdot 1=2$.

prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=4$, the graph shows $x(\tau)=3$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$ and $h(4-\tau)=2$ on $2\le \tau\le 5$, with both signals zero elsewhere.
Use the overlap area to find $y(4)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The supports overlap on $2\le \tau\le 4$, so the overlap width is 2. On that interval, the product height is $3\cdot 2=6$, giving area $6\cdot 2=12$.

sections.section_title: Reading Positive Overlap Area from Two Positive Signals

image_slots.image_description: Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared $\tau$-axis for fixed output time $t=4$. Top plot: $x(\tau)=1 on 0\le\tau\le5 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely above the axis. Middle plot: $h(4-\tau)=3 on 2\le\tau\le4 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely above the axis. Shade the overlap interval $2\le\tau\le4 on both plots$. Bottom product-area panel: show $x(\tau)$$h(4-\tau)$ as one positive shaded rectangle above the axis on $2\le\tau\le4$, zero elsewhere. Include $\tau$-axis labels and endpoints 0, 2, 4, and 5, and label the original signal heights 1 and 3. Do not include the numeric area label or $y(4)$ value.

Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared $\tau$-axis for fixed output time $t=5$. Top plot: $x(\tau)=2 on 1\le\tau\le5 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely above the axis. Middle plot: $h(5-\tau)=3 on 3\le\tau\le6 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely above the axis. Shade the overlap interval $3\le\tau\le5 on both plots$. Bottom product-area panel: show $x(\tau)$$h(5-\tau)$ as one positive shaded rectangle above the axis on $3\le\tau\le5$, zero elsewhere. Include $\tau$-axis labels and endpoints 1, 3, 5, and 6, and label the original signal heights 2 and 3. Do not include the numeric area label or $y(5)$ value.

prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=4$, the graph shows $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau\le 5$ and $h(4-\tau)=3$ on $2\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere.
Use the positive overlap area to find $y(4)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Both signals are positive on the overlap, so the product area adds to the output. The overlap is $2\le \tau\le 4$, with width 2, and the product height is $1\cdot 3=3$. Therefore $y(4)=3\cdot 2=6$.

prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=5$, the graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $1\le \tau\le 5$ and $h(5-\tau)=3$ on $3\le \tau\le 6$, with both signals zero elsewhere.
Use the positive overlap area to find $y(5)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Both overlapping signal values are above the axis, so the signed area is positive. The overlap is $3\le \tau\le 5$, with width 2, and the product height is $2\cdot 3=6$. Therefore $y(5)=6\cdot 2=12$.

sections.section_title: Accounting for Signed Area When the Product Is Negative

image_slots.image_description: Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared $\tau$-axis for fixed output time $t=1$. Top plot: $x(\tau)=3 on 0\le\tau\le2 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely above the axis. Middle plot: $h(1-\tau)=-1 on 1\le\tau\le4 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely below the axis on its support. Shade the overlap interval $1\le\tau\le2 on both plots$. Bottom product-area panel: show $x(\tau)$$h(1-\tau)$ as one shaded rectangle below the axis on $1\le\tau\le2$, zero elsewhere. Include $\tau$-axis labels and endpoints 0, 1, 2, and 4, and label the original signal heights 3 and -1. Do not include the numeric area label or $y(1)$ value.

Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared $\tau$-axis for fixed output time $t=4$. Top plot: $x(\tau)=2 on 1\le\tau\le5 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely above the axis. Middle plot: $h(4-\tau)=-3 on 3\le\tau\le6 and 0 elsewhere$, entirely below the axis on its support. Shade the overlap interval $3\le\tau\le5 on both plots$. Bottom product-area panel: show $x(\tau)$$h(4-\tau)$ as one shaded rectangle below the axis on $3\le\tau\le5$, zero elsewhere. prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=1$, the graph shows $x(\tau)=3$ on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(1-\tau)=-1$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere.
Use the signed overlap area to find $y(1)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The supports overlap on $1\le \tau\le 2$, so the overlap width is 1. On that interval, the product height is $3\cdot(-1)=-3$, which places the product below the axis. Therefore the signed area is $(-3)\cdot 1=-3$, so $y(1)=-3$.

prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=4$, the graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $1\le \tau\le 5$ and $h(4-\tau)=-3$ on $3\le \tau\le 6$, with both signals zero elsewhere.
Use the signed overlap area to find $y(4)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The supports overlap on $3\le \tau\le 5$, so the overlap width is 2. On that interval, the product height is $2\cdot(-3)=-6$, which is below the axis. Therefore the signed area is $(-6)\cdot 2=-12$, so $y(4)=-12$.

sections.section_title: Comparing Output Values from Different Amounts of Overlap

image_slots.image_description: Two side-by-side fixed-output-time panels on aligned $\tau$-axes. In both panels, show the same $x(\tau)=1 on 0\le\tau\le5 and 0 elsewhere$. Left panel labeled $t=1$: show $h(1-\tau)=4 on -1\le\tau\le2 and 0 elsewhere$, shade overlap $0\le\tau\le2$, and show a product-area rectangle $x(\tau)$$h(1-\tau)=4 above the axis on 0\le\tau\le2$. Right panel labeled $t=4$: show $h(4-\tau)=1 on 2\le\tau\le5 and 0 elsewhere$, shade overlap $2\le\tau\le5$, and show a product-area rectangle $x(\tau)$$h(4-\tau)=1 above the axis on 2\le\tau\le5$. Include endpoint labels -1, 0, 2, 5 and the product heights 4 and 1. Do not include numeric area values, output values, or the final comparison.

Two side-by-side fixed-output-time panels on aligned $\tau$-axes. In both panels, show the same $x(\tau)=2 on 0\le\tau\le4 and 0 elsewhere$. Left panel labeled $t=2$: show $h(2-\tau)=1 on 1\le\tau\le3 and 0 elsewhere$, shade overlap $1\le\tau\le3$, and show a product-area rectangle $x(\tau)$$h(2-\tau)=2 above the axis on 1\le\tau\le3$. Right panel labeled $t=5$: show $h(5-\tau)=-1 on 2\le\tau\le5 and 0 elsewhere$, shade overlap $2\le\tau\le4$, and show a product-area rectangle $x(\tau)$$h(5-\tau)=-2 below the axis on 2\le\tau\le4$. Include endpoint labels 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and product heights 2 and -2. Do not include numeric area values, output values, or the final comparison.

prompt_blocks.text: Two panels use the same input $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau\le 5$. In the first panel, $h(1-\tau)=4$ on $-1\le \tau\le 2$. In the second panel, $h(4-\tau)=1$ on $2\le \tau\le 5$. All signals are zero elsewhere.
Which comparison between $y(1)$ and $y(4)$ is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Both outputs are zero because the shifted responses differ.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $t=1$, the overlap is $0\le \tau\le 2$, so the width is 2 and the product height is $1\cdot 4=4$, giving area 8. For $t=4$, the overlap is $2\le \tau\le 5$, so the width is 3 and the product height is $1\cdot 1=1$, giving area 3. Since $8>3$, $y(1)>y(4)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Two panels use the same input $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 4$. In the first panel, $h(2-\tau)=1$ on $1\le \tau\le 3$. In the second panel, $h(5-\tau)=-1$ on $2\le \tau\le 5$. All signals are zero elsewhere.
Which comparison between $y(2)$ and $y(5)$ is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Both outputs are zero because the overlaps have equal width.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $t=2$, the overlap is $1\le \tau\le 3$, so the width is 2 and the product height is $2\cdot 1=2$, giving signed area $+4$. For $t=5$, the overlap is $2\le \tau\le 4$, so the width is 2 and the product height is $2\cdot(-1)=-2$, giving signed area $-4$. Since $4>-4$, $y(2)>y(5)$.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero Output from No Overlap Area

Middle plot: $h(6-\tau)$ is supported on $4\le\tau\le5 and zero elsewhere$. Leave a visible gap between $\tau=3 and \tau=4 and label it no overlap$. Do not shade any common interval. Bottom product-area panel: show the product signal lying on the zero axis for all $\tau$, with no product rectangle. Include $\tau$-axis labels and endpoints 1, 3, 4, and 5. Do not include a numeric area label or $y(6)$ value.

Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared $\tau$-axis for fixed output time $t=2$. Top plot: $x(\tau)$ is supported on $3\le\tau\le6 and zero elsewhere$. Middle plot: $h(2-\tau)$ is supported on $0\le\tau\le2 and zero elsewhere$. Leave a visible gap between $\tau=2 and \tau=3 and label it no overlap$. Do not shade any common interval. Do not include a numeric area label or $y(2)$ value.

prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=6$, a graph shows $x(\tau)$ supported on $1\le \tau\le 3$ and $h(6-\tau)$ supported on $4\le \tau\le 5$, with no overlap.
What is $y(6)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The two support intervals are separated: $[1,3]\cap[4,5]=\varnothing$. Since there is no $\tau$-value where both factors are nonzero, $x(\tau)h(6-\tau)=0$ for every $\tau$. The product area is therefore zero, so $y(6)=0$.

prompt_blocks.text: At fixed output time $t=2$, a graph shows $x(\tau)$ supported on $3\le \tau\le 6$ and $h(2-\tau)$ supported on $0\le \tau\le 2$, with no overlap.
What is $y(2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support intervals do not share any $\tau$-values: $[3,6]\cap[0,2]=\varnothing$. The output is not the area of one signal or the gap length; it is the signed area of the product. Because the product is zero everywhere, $y(2)=0$.
